label: Randall Lineback

about.text: The Randall Lineback is a rare American breed of color-sided cattle from Bennington County, Vermont, kept for milk, meat and draft work. It is now conserved by The Livestock Conservancy, which lists it as critical, and it is seldom milked today. Preliminary tests on its milk show about 3.7% butterfat and 3.2% protein.

sources.text: Wikipedia: Bennington County, Vermont; 'an all-purpose breed', used originally for dairy, meat and draft work. The Livestock Conservancy: 'Originally triple purpose but few milk them today'; listed as critical; most of the breed's population was lost over the last century through crossbreeding with Holsteins. The Dairy Site: 'Preliminary tests on their milk show an average of 3.7% Butter fat and 3.2% protein.' The 'about' sentences restate these; the 'critical' status is the Conservancy's.

origin.place: Bennington County, Vermont, from traditional color-sided cattle of New England

sources.text: Wikipedia: the breed derives from traditional color-sided cattle in New England; a herd was kept on the Randall family farm from 1912. The Livestock Conservancy: the lineback cattle of New England likely came from a mix of Dutch, English, Swedish and French stock, the name coming from the Randall family of Vermont. No formation date is given for the breed as a whole, so no 'formed' range is recorded.

Wikipedia: 'In 2015, the total number was over 500 head.' The article names no source for this. The count is the lower bound of 'over 500', and the milked flag is false because the figure is the total breed, not the milked animals.

The blog gives 'Average milk yield: 5,000 lbs annually (2,250 kg annually).' Its 2014 post date is used as the year. The figure is worked out from the blog's lb value (5,000 lb x 0.45359237 = 2,268 kg), not from its own kg value. One homestead blog is the only yield source found, so the confidence is low.
The Dairy Site: 'Preliminary tests on their milk show an average of 3.7% Butter fat and 3.2% protein.' Preliminary tests, a single average, so min and max hold the same value.

Wikipedia: 'Randall Cattle are an all-purpose breed', originally used for dairy, meat and draft work. The Livestock Conservancy: 'Linebacks were used for dairy and beef and as oxen.' Dual-purpose is the category for 'all-purpose'; draught from the oxen use. Dairy is left out of the ordering because the Conservancy says few are milked today.

Wikipedia: 'FAO (2007): endangered'; 'DAD-IS (2020): critical-maintained'; and The Livestock Conservancy lists it as 'critical' (with no year on its page). The DAD-IS record itself could not be opened (the country browse page returned 404), so the status is the Wikipedia article's report of DAD-IS 2020.

facts.v: In 1985 the herd was dispersed and many animals slaughtered. Six bulls and nine cows were bought for conservation and taken to Tennessee.

sources.text: Wikipedia: 'In 1985, it was dispersed, and many animals were slaughtered. Six bulls and nine cows were bought for conservation and taken to Tennessee.'

facts.v: A breed society was formed in 2005, and the breed became a State Heritage Breed of Vermont.

sources.text: Wikipedia: 'A breed society was formed in 2005', and the breed became a State Heritage Breed of Vermont.

facts.v: A lineback pattern of black markings on a white base. Blue, mahogany, gray and recessive reds have also been observed.

sources.text: Wikipedia: 'The coat is a lineback pattern of black markings on a white base. Blue, mahogany, gray, and recessive reds have also been observed.'

gaps: No DAD-IS record could be opened, so the population is the Wikipedia figure for 2015 with no source named, and the Livestock Conservancy gives no count or year. The milk yield rests on one homestead blog from 2014. The Livestock Conservancy page gives no milk yield, and no milk figure from a dairy-records body was found. The breed's formation date was not found.
